guide.title: San Saba, Rome: the Baths of Caracalla, Porta San Paolo and the Piccolo Aventino
guide.intro: San Saba is R. XXI, the twenty-first of Rome's rioni by toponymic code, and it is one of the two rioni, with Testaccio, that were carved out of Ripa in 1921, following Rome's first master plan of 1909. Romans call it il piccolo Aventino. Most of it is a quiet brick garden-suburb built between 1907 and 1914 by the Istituto Case Popolari, its streets named after architects and its stairways dropping to the Aurelian Walls. The rest is the Baths of Caracalla, four churches, a fifteenth-century villa on the old fork of the Appia and the Latina, the gate the via Ostiense began from, and two Novecento landmarks on the western and northern edges. Several of its boundaries are streets it shares with Celio, Ripa and Testaccio.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
No source states a metro station or a bus route for San Saba, so none is given here, and no source gives a walking time or a distance either. Steer by addresses.

The Soprintendenza Speciale di Roma gives the Baths of Caracalla as Viale delle Terme di Caracalla 52, 00153 Roma, with the site telephone 348 7964477. The Diocese of Rome gives Santi Nereo e Achilleo as Viale delle Terme di Caracalla 28. FAO's own contact page gives its headquarters as Viale delle Terme di Caracalla, 00153 Rome, telephone (+39) 06 57051; the building stands at the start of Viale Aventino, on the corner with Viale delle Terme di Caracalla. The parish gives Basilica di San Saba as Piazza Gian Lorenzo Bernini 20, telephone +39 06 64580140. Santa Balbina is Via di Santa Balbina 8, and its modern main approach is from Viale Guido Baccelli, up the Scalea Padre Simpliciano della Natività. The Stadio "Nando Martellini" is Viale Guido Baccelli 1.

Two addresses sit on boundary streets and are still addresses. San Cesareo de Appia is Via di Porta San Sebastiano 2, and the Casina del Cardinal Bessarione is on the same street, at the ancient fork of the via Appia and the via Latina, with no street number on the Sovrintendenza Capitolina's page. On the far side of the rione, the Palazzo delle Poste Roma Ostiense is Via Marmorata 4, and Porta San Paolo with the Museo della Via Ostiense inside it is on Via Raffaele Persichetti, the museum at number 3. The bookshop Il Mare is Via Leon Battista Alberti 1, and the three places to eat are all on the same two streets: Viale della Piramide Cestia 67 and 25, and Via di San Saba 30.

sections.heading: Opening times, tickets and what is shut
sections.body:
The Baths of Caracalla are the one full ticketed visit in the rione. The Soprintendenza Speciale di Roma gives them as closed Monday; 1 to 28 March 9.00 to 17.30, last admission 16.30; 29 March to 31 August 9.00 to 19.15, last admission 18.00; 1 to 30 September 9.00 to 19.00, last admission 18.00; 1 to 25 October 9.00 to 18.30, last admission 17.30; and 26 October to 28 February 9.00 to 16.30, last admission 15.30. Tickets are nominative and are sold only through the Musei Italiani portal, the Musei Italiani app, or the ticket desks and automatic totems on site. The Soprintendenza states that additional services such as guided visits or skip-the-line are not offered. The Domus di Vigna Guidi inside the precinct is included in the ordinary ticket, and the Soprintendenza states it is closed to the public on particularly crowded days, such as the first Sunday of the month, to protect the frescoes.

The churches vary. The parish of San Saba gives the basilica as Monday to Saturday 08.00 to 12.00 and 16.00 to 19.30, and Sunday and solemnities 09.00 to 13.00 and 16.00 to 19.30, with the parish office Monday to Friday 10.00 to 12.00. For Santi Nereo e Achilleo two institutions publish two answers: the Soprintendenza Speciale di Roma gives the opening as every Saturday 10.00 to 12.00, the Diocese of Rome's own record gives Tuesday and Thursday 9.00 to 12.00, and the two differ. For Santa Balbina, no source states its opening hours, so none are given here. San Cesareo de Appia cannot be entered at all: the Parco Archeologico dell'Appia Antica states that the site is currently visible from the street, and that restoration works under way will allow public access.

The Casina del Cardinal Bessarione runs on booking. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina admits groups only, on Saturday and Sunday, a maximum of fifteen per visit, with booking compulsory on 060608 between 09.00 and 19.00, and states that individual visits are also possible by booking on 060608 on a published calendar. It is closed Monday to Friday. Admission is 4.00 euro full and 3.00 euro reduced, free for residents of Rome and the metropolitan area on production of proof of residence and for MIC card holders; the guided visit is not included in the entry price and must be arranged separately. For the Museo della Via Ostiense, the Stadio "Nando Martellini", the bookshop and the three restaurants, no source states opening hours, so none are given here.

faq.question: What is actually in San Saba?
faq.answer: One very large archaeological site, the Baths of Caracalla, at Viale delle Terme di Caracalla 52. Four churches: the Basilica di San Saba that the rione is named for, Santa Balbina all'Aventino, Santi Nereo e Achilleo and San Cesareo de Appia. One Renaissance suburban villa, the Casina del Cardinal Bessarione. Porta San Paolo, with the Museo della Via Ostiense inside its Castelletto. Two buildings of the Fascist decades, the Palazzo delle Poste Roma Ostiense on Via Marmorata and the Palazzo FAO. Piazza Albania with its Scanderbeg monument, the Parco della Resistenza dell'Otto Settembre with the Fontana dell'Anfora, and the brick garden-quarter the Istituto Case Popolari built on the Piccolo Aventino.

faq.question: Is the Pyramid of Cestius in San Saba?
faq.answer: No. it.wikipedia files the Piramide di Caio Cestio under Rione XX Testaccio. The gate beside it, Porta San Paolo, is in San Saba: the Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that two gates originally flanked the Pyramid, built to ease traffic between the city and the port of Ostia, and that the western one was closed as the via Portuense took over and demolished in 1888. The Sovrintendenza also records that around 1920 the surviving gate was isolated from the Aurelian Walls to ease traffic on its eastern side, and that a bombing in the Second World War destroyed the western stretch of wall that linked it to the Pyramid.

faq.question: Where does the name San Saba come from, and what are the rione's arms?
faq.answer: The rione takes its name from the basilica. it.wikipedia's article on the rione records that hermits settled on the ruins of what was probably the statio of the fourth cohort of the vigiles, and that in the eighth century monks from the community founded at Jerusalem by St Sabas took the site. The same article gives the rione's popular name as il piccolo Aventino, and its arms, citing Pietrangeli's Insegne e stemmi dei rioni di Roma of 1953, as azure, a silver crescent in chief and Diana's silver bow in base, alluding to Diana Aventina.

faq.question: Can you go inside San Cesareo de Appia?
faq.answer: Not at present. The Parco Archeologico dell'Appia Antica states that the site is currently visible from the street, and that restoration works under way will allow public access. The Parco also states that the church has been state property since 1959, and that it passed from the Direzione musei statali della città di Roma to the Parco because of where it stands, on Via di Porta San Sebastiano along the first mile of the Appia. What you can see from the street is a severe façade with sparse columns and pilasters and wide blind panels.

faq.question: How do you visit the Casina del Cardinal Bessarione?
faq.answer: By booking. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina admits groups only, on Saturday and Sunday, a maximum of fifteen per visit, with booking compulsory on 060608 between 09.00 and 19.00, and states that individual visits are also possible by booking on 060608 on a published calendar. It is closed Monday to Friday. Admission is 4.00 euro full and 3.00 euro reduced, free for residents of Rome and the metropolitan area on production of proof of residence and for MIC card holders, and the guided visit is not included in the entry price. The Sovrintendenza gives the street without a number: Via di Porta San Sebastiano, at the ancient fork of the via Appia and the via Latina.

faq.question: Is there anything to do in San Saba in the evening?
faq.answer: Three places to eat: Taverna Cestia at Viale della Piramide Cestia 67, Baccio e i gradini at Viale della Piramide Cestia 25, and Saba Caffè & Cucina at Via di San Saba 30. None of the three publishes its opening hours, so none are given here. Beyond them the rione is residential: the Istituto Case Popolari quarter, the Parco della Resistenza dell'Otto Settembre and Piazza Albania are open ground you can walk through, and the bookshop Il Mare on Via Leon Battista Alberti sells nautical and geographic charts and prints them to custom sizes.

photos.title: Porta San Paolo
photos.description: The outer face of Porta San Paolo, the gate the via Ostiense began from, with the single entrance fornix and the two merlonated flanking towers raised by Honorius, and the banner of the Museo della Via Ostiense over the arch.
photos.author: Dietmar Rabich

places.name: Terme di Caracalla
places.address: Viale delle Terme di Caracalla 52, 00153 Roma RM
places.summary: An imperial bath complex on three descending terraces. The Soprintendenza Speciale di Roma describes a rectangular outer precinct, holding two symmetrical libraries on the south side, latrines east and west and the cisterns, enclosing a central block laid out on a single axis: calidarium, tepidarium, frigidarium and the natatio, which was open to the sky, with two palestre and the changing rooms symmetrically east and west and an upper floor over the palestre used for depilation and massage. The main entrances were on the north front, over tabernae opening onto the via Nova. About two kilometres of underground galleries run beneath, carrying the furnaces and boilers, a water plant, a mill and a Mithraeum with its fossa sanguinis. The Soprintendenza gives the hours as closed Monday; 1 to 28 March 9.00 to 17.30, last admission 16.30; 29 March to 31 August 9.00 to 19.15, last admission 18.00; 1 to 30 September 9.00 to 19.00, last admission 18.00; 1 to 25 October 9.00 to 18.30, last admission 17.30; 26 October to 28 February 9.00 to 16.30, last admission 15.30. Tickets are nominative and are sold only through the Musei Italiani portal, the Musei Italiani app, or the ticket desks and automatic totems on site. The Soprintendenza states that additional services such as guided visits or skip-the-line are not offered. Site telephone 348 7964477; the responsabile is Dott. Rocco Bochicchio.
places.history: Built for Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Bassianus, called Caracalla, and inaugurated in 216 AD. The Soprintendenza Speciale di Roma states that the baths were built in five years, that the works continued past Caracalla's death in 217 and were finished under Elagabalus and Alexander Severus, and that the complex was restored above all under Constantine. It was supplied by the Aqua Antoniniana, an aqueduct branch built for it, and stopped working in 537 AD, when Vitiges cut the aqueducts during the Gothic siege. On the south-east side of the complex is the Domus di Vigna Guidi, discovered between 1858 and 1869 by Giovan Battista Guidi, honorary inspector of Ancient Monuments, covered over, then excavated and studied again from 1970, and returned to display in 2022 after restoration; a sacello there shows the Egyptian deities Anubis, Isis and probably Osiris, facing Jupiter, Juno and Minerva. It is included in the ordinary ticket, and the Soprintendenza states it is closed to the public on particularly crowded days, such as the first Sunday of the month, to protect the frescoes. The Teatro dell'Opera di Roma programmes a Caracalla Festival, which it lists as a strand of its season.

places.name: Basilica di San Saba
places.address: Piazza Gian Lorenzo Bernini 20, 00153 Roma RM
places.summary: The church the rione is named for, on the Piccolo Aventino, served by a Jesuit community that lives in the adjoining monastery. The parish gives its address as Parrocchia San Saba, Piazza Gian Lorenzo Bernini 20, 00153 Roma. The parish office is inside the basilica, through the door at the end of the right-hand nave, with an entrance on Via di San Saba; it can also be reached from the rear entrance at Piazza Gian Lorenzo Bernini 20. The parish gives the basilica as open Monday to Saturday 08.00 to 12.00 and 16.00 to 19.30, and Sunday and solemnities 09.00 to 13.00 and 16.00 to 19.30; the parish office Monday to Friday 10.00 to 12.00; the Rosary daily at 18.00; and Mass on weekdays at 09.00 and 18.30 and on Sundays and solemnities at 10.30, 12.00 and 18.30. Telephone +39 06 64580140.
places.history: it.wikipedia's article on the rione records that hermits settled here on the ruins of what was probably the statio of the fourth cohort of the vigiles, and that in the eighth century monks from the community founded at Jerusalem by St Sabas took the site and founded a monastery. Its holdings included the castles of Marino and Palo. The community passed from the Benedictines to the Cluniacs, then to the Cistercians, and from 1573 to the Collegio Germanico-Ungarico under the Jesuits, who hold it today. The monastery is the same complex as the church.

places.name: Basilica di Santa Balbina all'Aventino
places.address: Via di Santa Balbina 8, 00153 Roma RM
places.summary: A hall church: a single space without aisles, with alternating rectangular and semicircular side chapels set between piers, some of them frescoed. it.wikipedia's article on the church records ancient Roman mosaics from the via dei Fori Imperiali excavations laid in the floor in the 1930s, a Cosmatesque episcopal cathedra in the apse, and apse frescoes, a Gloria di Cristo with Ss Felicissimus, Balbina, Quirinus and a holy pontiff, with St Peter and St Paul on the triumphal arch, painted by Anastasio Fontebuoni in 1600 for Cardinal Pompeo Arrigoni, titular from 1597. The present façade is a sixteenth-century remaking. The postal address is Via di Santa Balbina 8; the modern main approach is from Viale Guido Baccelli, up the Scalea Padre Simpliciano della Natività. It is not a parish. It is a place of worship and a filial church of the Basilica di San Pietro in Vaticano. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The masonry, opera listata and brick, suggests the fourth century, but the building may have begun as part of a rich domus, identified from brick stamps as the house Septimius Severus gave to Lucius Fabius Cilo, twice consul and Prefect of Rome, at the start of the third century. The first attestation of the titulus is the synod of 595. it.wikipedia records the church as a minor basilica, which is an ecclesiastical rank. The adjoining fortified convent is dedicated to St Margaret of Cortona and is run as a hospice by the Suore Francescane dei Sacri Cuori, founded by Padre Simpliciano della Natività, for whom the stair up from Viale Guido Baccelli is named. It houses elderly and socially vulnerable residents.

places.name: Chiesa dei Santi Nereo e Achilleo
places.address: Viale delle Terme di Caracalla 28, 00153 Roma RM
places.summary: A church of three naves with a wooden roof. The Soprintendenza Speciale di Roma records the mosaic outside the apsidal arch, an Annunciation, a Transfiguration and a Theotokos, as surviving decoration of the time of Leo III; the two side altarpieces in situ, Durante Alberti's Madonna adored by angels on the right and Cristoforo Roncalli il Pomarancio's Ss Nereus, Achilleus and Domitilla on the left; and the relics of the martyrs in an urn still under the high altar. The façade opens onto a small forecourt on Viale delle Terme di Caracalla and keeps the form given it by the restorations of Sixtus IV. It is a gabled front carrying geometric sgraffito decoration, which it.wikipedia attributes to Girolamo Massei, commissioned by Cardinal Cesare Baronio. The façade was restored in 2025. The Soprintendenza Speciale di Roma gives the opening as every Saturday 10.00 to 12.00. The Diocese of Rome's own record gives Tuesday and Thursday 9.00 to 12.00. The two differ. The Diocese records the church as a rectory of the parish of Santa Maria in Vallicella, with Fr Simone Raponi as rector from 01/07/2022.
places.history: The Soprintendenza Speciale di Roma records the titulus fasciolae, instituted under Julius I (337 to 352); the titulus later took the martyrs' names and is so recorded in a letter of Gregory the Great in 600. A basilican church was built under Leo III (795 to 816), then abandoned as the site was unhealthy, and ruined. Sixtus IV (1471 to 1484) transformed it shortly before the Holy Year, removing the first two bays and replacing the dividing columns with octagonal masonry piers, and raised it to a cardinal's title. Cardinal Cesare Baronio of the Roman Oratory had the church restored and decorated in 1597, ahead of the Jubilee of 1600, when the relics of Ss Nereus, Achilleus and Domitilla were translated here.

places.name: Chiesa di San Cesareo de Appia
places.address: Via di Porta San Sebastiano 2, 00153 Roma RM
places.summary: A church on the first mile of the Appia whose forms were defined at the start of the seventeenth century under Clement VIII Aldobrandini. The Parco Archeologico dell'Appia Antica describes a coffered wooden ceiling and a nave painting cycle ascribed to the Cavalier d'Arpino, Cosmatesque presbytery furnishings brought from San Giovanni in Laterano, extensive mosaic decoration, and a severe façade with sparse columns and pilasters and wide blind panels. Beneath the church is an imperial-age space of the second century AD, probably a bath building, found in the mid-1930s, with an extensive marine-motif mosaic floor. The Parco Archeologico dell'Appia Antica states that the site is currently visible from the street, and that restoration works under way will allow public access.
places.history: The Parco Archeologico dell'Appia Antica states that the church has been state property since 1959, and that it passed from the Direzione musei statali della città di Roma to the Parco because of where it stands, on Via di Porta San Sebastiano along the first mile of the Appia.

places.name: Casina del Cardinal Bessarione
places.address: Via di Porta San Sebastiano, 00153 Roma RM
places.summary: A suburban villa with an Italianate garden, on Via di Porta San Sebastiano, at the ancient fork of the via Appia and the via Latina. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives no street number for it. It admits groups only, on Saturday and Sunday, a maximum of fifteen per visit, with booking compulsory on 060608 between 09.00 and 19.00; individual visits are also possible by booking on 060608 on a published calendar. It is closed Monday to Friday. Admission is 4.00 euro full and 3.00 euro reduced, free for residents of Rome and the metropolitan area on production of proof of residence and free for MIC card holders; the guided visit is not included in the entry price and must be arranged separately.
places.history: The present form is fifteenth-century, over medieval fabric that itself encloses Roman structures. Below the basement are funerary structures of the first century BC and a building of at least three phases, from the early imperial period to the first half of the second century AD, from which survive black-and-white mosaic paving and an opus mixtum wall in the ground-floor south-west masonry. The medieval phase relates to a hospital run in the early fourteenth century by the fratres cruciferi, later a Benedictine nunnery. The extension towards the street with the first-floor loggia, and the conversion into the summer residence of the cardinal titular of Tusculum, date to the second half of the fifteenth century. From this comes the hypothesis, which the Sovrintendenza Capitolina says recent documentary finds support, that Cardinal Giovanni Bessarione, titular of Tusculum from 1449 to 1468, lived here. Clement VIII granted it in 1600 to the Collegio Clementino, which he had founded in 1594; after the college was suppressed in 1870 it passed to the Convitto Nazionale, was reduced to an inn between the late 1800s and the early 1900s, was ceded by the State to the Comune di Roma in 1926, and was restored and inaugurated in 1933. It is now one of the Comune's representative venues.

places.name: Porta San Paolo
places.summary: A gate of the Aurelian Walls, and the point the via Ostiense began from. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that two gates originally flanked the Pyramid of Cestius, built to ease traffic between the city and the port of Ostia, and that the western one, running towards the granaries of the Marmorata on the Tiber bank, was closed as the via Portuense took over and was demolished in 1888. The surviving gate's Roman name was Porta Ostiensis; it was renamed for the road out to San Paolo fuori le Mura. Inside it, in the Castelletto, is the Museo della Via Ostiense.
places.history: Between 401 and 403 Honorius restructured the gate, keeping a single entrance fornix and reinforcing and raising the two flanking towers, giving them merlons and windows. A restoration under Benedict XIV in 1749 took in the whole Roman circuit from Porta San Paolo to Porta Flaminia, and is recorded by a commemorative inscription on the eastern tower. Around 1920 the gate was isolated from the Aurelian Walls to ease traffic on its eastern side, and a bombing in the Second World War destroyed the western stretch of wall that linked it to the Pyramid. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that on 10 September 1943 Porta San Paolo was the scene of the last attempt by the Italian army and Roman civilians to prevent the German occupation of Rome.

places.name: Museo della Via Ostiense
places.summary: A museum inside Porta San Paolo, at Via Raffaele Persichetti 3. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina states that it occupies the Castelletto, the counter-gate built like a small fortification by Maxentius at the start of the fourth century AD, that it is run by the Soprintendenza Speciale di Roma, and that it displays reconstructions of the ports of Ostia and of monuments found along the via Ostiensis. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.

places.name: Palazzo delle Poste Roma Ostiense
places.summary: A post office building of the 1930s on Via Marmorata: symmetrical, standing on a wide flight of steps, laid out on geometric ratios and the golden section, with three volumes in a U, faced in smooth white marble, a portico closing the rectangular court on the front, and end blocks carrying a crossed-diagonal motif that masks the internal stairs. It houses the Roma Ostiense post office, frazionario 55645. it.wikipedia's article on the building says it is situated in via Marmorata, in rione San Saba.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the 1932 competition called by the Ministero delle comunicazioni was won by Adalberto Libera, that the building went up between 1933 and 1935 and was inaugurated on 28 October 1935. It also records that Libera and Mario De Renzi entered designs for four post offices in the same competition, two signed by each, because the rules required a single signatory, and that De Renzi was only later established as co-author of the Via Marmorata building.

places.name: Palazzo FAO
places.address: Viale delle Terme di Caracalla, 00153 Roma RM
places.summary: The headquarters of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, standing at the start of Viale Aventino on the corner with Viale delle Terme di Caracalla. FAO's own contact page gives the address as Viale delle Terme di Caracalla, 00153 Rome, and the telephone as (+39) 06 57051. No source states a public visiting arrangement, so none is given here.
places.history: Designed by Vittorio Cafiero and Mario Ridolfi and begun in 1938 as the seat of the Ministero dell'Africa Italiana, formerly the Ministero delle Colonie, which was abolished in 1953, it was finished after the war and given to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, whose headquarters it is. it.wikipedia's article on the rione records that Viale Aventino, opened in those years, was originally named Viale Africa, and that the name later passed to a street in EUR.

places.name: Piazza Albania and the Monumento a Giorgio Castriota Scanderbeg
places.summary: A square on the western side of the rione, with an equestrian bronze of Giorgio Castriota Scanderbeg (1403 to 1468) on a semi-oval pedestal above a rectangular travertine base. He rides at a walk in traditional Albanian dress, wearing the two-horned helmet whose goat protome carries long horns, a drawn sword raised in his right hand. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina states that the monument was unveiled in Piazza Albania by Benito Mussolini on 27 October 1940. it.wikipedia gives the sculptor as Romano Romanelli.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina states that the square was formerly known as Piazza Raudusculana, after the gate that opened here in the stretch of the Servian Walls, and had recently been renamed Piazza Albania in connection with the annexation of Albania to the Kingdom of Italy in 1939. A commemorative epigraph was placed on the main face of the base in 1968 by the Amministrazione capitolina, for the fifth centenary of the condottiero's death.

places.name: Parco della Resistenza dell'Otto Settembre
places.summary: A public park behind the Palazzo delle Poste, bounded by Piazza Albania, Via della Piramide Cestia, Via Marmorata and Viale Manlio Gelsomini. In it stands the Fontana dell'Anfora, also to Raffaele de Vico's design: a wide circular basin at ground level with an octagonal travertine base carrying a bronze amphora with eight spouts like raised trunks, a central jet, and eight holes in the belly of the vessel. It is not the Fontana delle Anfore by Pietro Lombardi, which is a different fountain, in Testaccio.
places.history: Roma Segreta records that the park was inaugurated on 21 April 1939 to a design by Raffaele de Vico. It was laid out as Parco Cestio, for the Pyramid of Cestius, and later renamed for the Resistance of September 1943 at Porta San Paolo. The same account records that the name Parco Cestio stayed with the small green patch on the other side of Via Marmorata, which belongs to Rione XX Testaccio.

places.name: Quartiere ICP del Piccolo Aventino
places.summary: The brick garden-quarter that fills most of the rione, between the basilica and the Aurelian Walls. it.wikipedia's article on the rione describes two-family villini each with a small garden, and blocks of no more than four floors with courtyards, each faced in brick the colour of the old brickwork of the church and the walls. The streets are named after architects: Bernini, Borromini, Baccio Pontelli, Palladio, Pirro Ligorio, Bramante. The site is a plateau on a hilltop, crossed by ramps and stairways dropping to the walls or to Testaccio below. Via Baccio Pontelli and Via Andrea Palladio are stairways, and Viale Giotto runs along the inside face of the Aurelian Walls.
places.history: Between 1907 and 1914 the Blocco Popolare governing the city, radicals, republicans and socialists under mayor Ernesto Nathan, had the Istituto Case Popolari build ten lots of housing on the Piccolo Aventino, for the salaried lower-middle class. The area had been zoned as public green by the post-1870 master plan, next to the Passeggiata Archeologica. It was designed, like the ICP housing in Testaccio, by the then-young Quadrio Pirani. San Saba and Testaccio were carved out of Ripa in 1921, following Rome's first master plan of 1909. it.wikipedia reproduces an inscription on a cippus walled into the façade of a 1930 apartment building in the quarter, recording that Augustus made public the land on which the newer part of the rione stands: ID QVOD INTRA CIPPOS AD CAMPVM VERSVS SOLI EST CAESAR AVGVSTVS REDEMPTVM A PRIVATO PVBLICAVIT.

places.name: Libreria Internazionale Il Mare
places.address: Via Leon Battista Alberti 1, 00153 Roma RM
places.summary: A bookshop specialising in the sea, trading as Oltremare Srl at Via Leon Battista Alberti 1. Its departments are books, nautical charts, electronic charts, fishing charts, geographic charts, globes, instruments and prints, and it prints nautical and geographic charts to custom sizes. The shop states it carries over 30,000 titles. Email ilmare@ilmare.com, telephone +39 3476141118. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The shop's own site gives its address as via Leon Battista Alberti 1, Rione San Saba, 00153 Roma, naming the rione itself.

places.name: Stadio "Nando Martellini" (Terme di Caracalla)
places.summary: An athletics stadium at Viale Guido Baccelli 1. No source states its opening or event arrangements, so none are given here.
places.history: it.wikipedia's article on Santa Balbina refers to it as the modern Stadio delle Terme.

places.name: Taverna Cestia
places.address: Viale della Piramide Cestia 67, 00153 Roma RM
places.summary: A restaurant on Viale della Piramide Cestia. Its own site gives Roman cooking and pizza it describes as bassa e scrocchiarella, and says private functions are taken by enquiry. Telephone 06 57 43 754 or 393 6106061. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.

places.name: Baccio e i gradini
places.address: Viale della Piramide Cestia 25, 00153 Roma RM
places.summary: A restaurant at Viale della Piramide Cestia 25. Its own site gives pizza, fritti and beer, and takes bookings by WhatsApp. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.

places.name: Saba Caffè & Cucina
places.address: Via di San Saba 30, 00153 Roma RM
places.summary: A restaurant and pinseria at Via di San Saba 30, on the street the rione is named for. Its own site is the source for the name and the address. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.

entries.name: Terme di Caracalla
entries.note: Inaugurated in 216 AD and out of use from 537 AD, when Vitiges cut the aqueducts; about two kilometres of service galleries run under the precinct.

entries.name: Buy the Caracalla ticket before you go
entries.note: The Soprintendenza sells nominative tickets only through the Musei Italiani portal, the Musei Italiani app, or the desks and totems on site, and offers no skip-the-line.

entries.name: Basilica di San Saba
entries.note: The church the rione is named for, held since 1573 by the Collegio Germanico-Ungarico under the Jesuits, who serve it today; open from 08.00 on weekday mornings.

entries.name: Basilica di Santa Balbina all'Aventino
entries.note: A hall church with Roman floor mosaics laid in the 1930s and apse frescoes of 1600 by Anastasio Fontebuoni; no source states its opening hours.

entries.name: Chiesa dei Santi Nereo e Achilleo
entries.note: Rebuilt by Sixtus IV and redecorated in 1597 for Cardinal Baronio; the Soprintendenza gives Saturday 10.00 to 12.00 and the Diocese Tuesday and Thursday 9.00 to 12.00.

entries.name: Chiesa di San Cesareo de Appia
entries.note: The Parco Archeologico dell'Appia Antica states the church is currently visible from the street, with restoration works under way that will allow public access.

entries.name: Casina del Cardinal Bessarione
entries.note: A fifteenth-century villa open Saturdays and Sundays to booked groups of fifteen, on 060608; 4.00 euro full, 3.00 euro reduced, guided visit arranged separately.

entries.name: Porta San Paolo
entries.note: The gate the via Ostiense began from, known to the Romans as Porta Ostiensis and restructured by Honorius between 401 and 403 to a single entrance fornix.

entries.name: Museo della Via Ostiense
entries.note: Inside the Castelletto of Porta San Paolo: reconstructions of the ports of Ostia and of monuments found along the via Ostiensis. No source states its hours.

entries.name: Palazzo delle Poste Roma Ostiense
entries.note: Adalberto Libera's competition-winning post office of 1933 to 1935 on Via Marmorata, in white marble on a wide flight of steps, still a working post office.

entries.name: Quartiere ICP del Piccolo Aventino
entries.note: Ten lots of Istituto Case Popolari housing built 1907 to 1914 to Quadrio Pirani's designs, on streets named for architects, with stairways down to the walls.

entries.name: Parco della Resistenza dell'Otto Settembre
entries.note: Raffaele de Vico's park of 21 April 1939, laid out as Parco Cestio, holding his Fontana dell'Anfora with its bronze amphora and eight raised spouts.

entries.name: Piazza Albania and the Scanderbeg monument
entries.note: Formerly Piazza Raudusculana, after the Servian Walls gate here; the equestrian bronze was unveiled on 27 October 1940 by Benito Mussolini.

entries.name: Taverna Cestia
entries.note: Roman cooking and pizza the restaurant's own site calls bassa e scrocchiarella, on Viale della Piramide Cestia; private functions taken by enquiry.
